title: Project Architecture
text:
Repository design · reproducibility · validation
    

    

    
      This page explains how the NHANES Laboratory Data with R project is
      organized technically. It focuses on repository structure, reproducible
      execution, modular R code, validation contracts, provenance, output
      management, testing, versioning, and extension.
    

    

      
        Educational layer
        
          Foundations, laboratory guides, pipeline catalogs, and structured courses
        
      

      
        Execution layer
        
          Configuration files, R functions, scripts, validation rules, and tests
        
      

      
        Output layer
        
          Processed datasets, tables, figures, logs, and provenance records

Install the missing package:

  "package_name"
)
Exit R:

Then rerun the package check.






WarningDo not install packages repeatedly inside the production pipeline



Package installation is an environment-setup task.
The production pipeline should validate and load packages, not reinstall them every time it runs.

    minimum_interval =
      min(
        lower_descriptive_95,
        na.rm = TRUE
      ),
    maximum_interval =
      max(
        upper_descriptive_95,
        na.rm = TRUE

title: Lesson 19: Troubleshoot Common Pipeline Problems

  ylim = c(
    trend_y_axis_lower,
    trend_y_axis_upper
  )
)
only when the limits contain every plotted mean and interval.

text:
Create the principal figure
Run:
hemoglobin_trend_plot <-
  ggplot2::ggplot(
    hemoglobin_trend_figure_data,
    ggplot2::aes(
      x = survey_cycle_factor,
      y = mean_hemoglobin,
      group = sex,
      color = sex,
      shape = sex
    )
  ) +
  ggplot2::geom_errorbar(
    ggplot2::aes(
      ymin = lower_descriptive_95,

    width = 0.12,
    linewidth = 0.55,
    position = ggplot2::position_dodge(
      width = 0.16
    )
  ) +
  ggplot2::geom_line(
    linewidth = 1.05,
    position = ggplot2::position_dodge(
      width = 0.16
    )
  ) +
  ggplot2::geom_point(
    size = 3.1,
    stroke = 0.8,
    position = ggplot2::position_dodge(
      width = 0.16
    )
  ) +
  ggplot2::annotate(
    geom = "label",
    x = trend_annotation_x,
    y = trend_annotation_y,
    label = trend_caveat_text,
    hjust = 0,
    vjust = 1,
    size = 3.25,
    fontface = "bold",
    lineheight = 1.05,
    fill = "white",
    color = "black",
    label.size = 0.4,
    label.padding = grid::unit(
      0.18,
      "lines"
    )
  ) +
  ggplot2::scale_color_manual(
    values = hemoglobin_palette,
    breaks = c(
      "Male",
      "Female"
    )
  ) +
  ggplot2::scale_shape_manual(
    values = hemoglobin_shapes,
    breaks = c(
      "Male",
      "Female"
    )
  ) +
  ggplot2::scale_y_continuous(
    breaks = seq(
      trend_y_axis_lower,
      trend_y_axis_upper,
      by = trend_y_axis_break
    ),
    labels = scales::label_number(
      accuracy = 0.1
    ),
    expand = ggplot2::expansion(
      mult = c(
        0,
        0
      )
    )
  ) +
  ggplot2::coord_cartesian(
    ylim = c(
      trend_y_axis_lower,
      trend_y_axis_upper
    ),
    clip = "off"
  ) +
  ggplot2::labs(
    title =
      "Mean Hemoglobin Concentration Across NHANES Survey Cycles",
    subtitle =
      "Unweighted descriptive means by sex, 1999–2018",
    x =
      "NHANES two-year survey cycle",
    y =
      hemoglobin_y_axis_label,
    color =
      "Sex",
    shape =
      "Sex",
    caption =
      paste(
        "Figure 1.",
        "Points represent unweighted group means and error bars represent conventional",
        "mean ± 1.96 standard-error intervals.",
        "The analysis does not incorporate NHANES sampling weights, SDMVSTRA,",
        "SDMVPSU, or complex-survey variance estimation.",
        "Results describe the analytical records and are not nationally representative."
      )
  ) +
  theme_hemoglobin_publication(
    base_size = 11
  )

title: Lesson 15: Save Reusable Outputs
text:
Common mistakes

Saving only CSV
CSV is portable but does not preserve R metadata.


Saving only RDS
RDS preserves metadata but may be less convenient for collaborators using other software.


Overwriting raw source files
Processed outputs should be stored separately from:
data/raw/


Failing to save validation reports
A dataset without its validation evidence is harder to audit.


Omitting package versions
Package behavior can change over time.

section: Validation does not replace scientific review

title: Lesson 13: Validate the Merged Results
text:
Common mistakes

Assuming a successful join is sufficient
A join can succeed while producing duplicate or incomplete records.


Treating all missing values as errors
Some missingness reflects eligibility, specimen collection, component availability, or cycle structure.


Deleting unusual laboratory values automatically
Unusual values should be flagged and investigated first.


Using one weight for every analysis
Weight selection depends on the component, subsample, cycles, and analytical population.


Validating only the final row count
Row counts are important, but keys, cycles, variables, provenance, match status, and value structure must also be checked.


Ignoring failed checks
A validation table is useful only when the pipeline stops or clearly warns when critical expectations are violated.

Knowledge check






NoteWhy should the final merged row count equal the primary CBC row count?





The merge uses the primary CBC dataset as the left analytical base. A one-to-one left join should add Demographic columns without adding or removing CBC rows.









NoteDoes an unusual hemoglobin value automatically mean the record should be deleted?





No. It should be flagged and investigated for measurement, coding, unit, method, or source issues before any exclusion decision is made.









NoteDoes passing pipeline validation make an unweighted analysis nationally representative?





No. National inference still requires the appropriate NHANES survey weights, strata, primary sampling units, and multi-cycle weighting procedures.

title: Understand NHANES Data
text:
Participant identifier: SEQN
SEQN is the respondent sequence number.
It is commonly used to link person-level NHANES files.
Within one survey cycle, a person-level merge may use:
dplyr::left_join(
  cbc_data,
  demographic_data,
  by = "SEQN"
)
After multiple cycles are combined, this project uses:
survey_cycle + SEQN
as the explicit analytic key.

title: Understand NHANES Data
section: Why include the survey cycle in the key?

title: Understand NHANES Data
text:
Survey-design variables
Important public-use design variables include:
SDMVSTRA
SDMVPSU
Common weight variables include:
WTINT2YR
WTMEC2YR
For some early combined periods, four-year weight variables may be required.
Specialized laboratory components may also contain component-specific subsample weights.






ImportantThere is no universal NHANES weight



The correct weight depends on:

the variables included;
the component with the smallest eligible sample;
whether the analysis uses a subsample;
the survey cycles combined;
the intended population estimate.

title: Understand NHANES Data
Understand NHANES Data
text:
One-to-one example
Suppose CBC and Demographics each contain one record per participant and cycle.
The intended relationship is:
one CBC record ↔ one Demographic record

title: Understand NHANES Data
text:
One-to-many example
A medication file may contain multiple prescriptions for one participant.
The relationship may be:
one participant ↔ several medication records
Joining such a file directly can increase the number of rows.

title: Understand NHANES Data
text:
Repeat-examination example
The 2001–2002 CBC release includes a second-examination file.
A participant may therefore have:

one primary CBC record;
one second-examination CBC record.

These records represent different examinations, not duplicate copies of one observation.

title: Understand NHANES Data
text:
Source-file names change over time
CBC filenames may include forms such as:
LAB25
L25_B
L25_C
CBC_D
CBC_E
CBC_F
CBC_G
CBC_H
CBC_I
CBC_J
Demographic filenames commonly follow forms such as:
DEMO
DEMO_B
DEMO_C
DEMO_D
DEMO_E
DEMO_F
DEMO_G
DEMO_H
DEMO_I
DEMO_J
The filename suffix identifies a release cycle, but the pipeline should store the human-readable cycle label explicitly.

title: Understand NHANES Data

File format
NHANES public-use files are commonly released as SAS transport files:
.xpt
R reads them using:
haven::read_xpt()

title: Understand NHANES Data
text:
Labels and imported data
XPT files can contain variable labels and labelled values.
When imported through haven, some columns may use the class:
haven_labelled
The pipeline should preserve the source variables while creating readable analytical variables later.

title: NHANES Laboratory Data
text:
Laboratory science · survey data · reproducibility
    

    
      Laboratory results become evidence only after their context is preserved.
    

    
      NHANES laboratory files connect specimen collection, analytical methods,
      quality assurance, participant eligibility, survey design, and public-use
      data. This section explains how to move from a released laboratory file
      to a scientifically defensible analytical dataset.
    

    

      
        Specimen context
        Collection, handling, storage, and eligibility
      

      
        Method context
        Instrument, procedure, calibration, and quality control
      

      
        Data context
        Variables, units, detection limits, and missingness
      

      
        Survey context
        Weights, strata, PSUs, cycles, and target population
      

    

  


The laboratory data journey
Laboratory data pass through several scientific and operational stages before appearing in an NHANES XPT file.


  
    1
    Eligibility
    Determine who qualifies for the examination or laboratory component.
  

  
    2
    Collection
    Obtain blood, urine, or another specimen under defined procedures.
  

  
    3
    Handling
    Process, label, store, and transport the specimen appropriately.
  

  
    4
    Measurement
    Analyze the specimen using a documented laboratory method.
  

  
    5
    Quality review
    Apply calibration, controls, flags, and analytical validation.
  

  
    6
    Public release
    Publish variables, documentation, weights, and analytical guidance.
  








ImportantThe released value is the final stage, not the whole story



A laboratory result should be interpreted together with:

who was eligible;
how the specimen was collected;
how the method worked;
what units were reported;
whether limits of detection applied;
which survey weight represents the tested population.





Four laboratory-data principles


  
    Methods matter
    
      The same analyte may be measured using different instruments, procedures,
      calibration systems, or laboratory sites across survey cycles.
    
  

  
    Eligibility defines the sample
    
      Not every participant is eligible for every laboratory component.
      Age, examination status, fasting, session, or subsample selection may apply.
    
  

  
    Units must be verified
    
      A familiar variable name does not guarantee that units, coding,
      reporting limits, or interpretation remained unchanged.
    
  

  
    Provenance must survive
    
      Every analytical record should retain its survey cycle, source file,
      component, variable origin, and processing history.
    
  




Explore laboratory component types
Select a category to see how its analytical considerations may differ.


  

    
      Hematology
    

    
      Clinical chemistry
    

    
      Exposure biomarkers
    

    
      Infectious disease
    

    
      Nutrition biomarkers
    

  

  
    Hematology

    
      Hematology components may include complete blood count variables such as
      hemoglobin, hematocrit, erythrocyte indices, leukocyte counts, and platelets.
    

    
      Review analyzer and method changes across cycles.
      Verify units and age-specific interpretation.
      Distinguish primary and repeat examinations.
      Retain specimen and cycle provenance.
    
  

  
    Clinical chemistry

    
      Chemistry components may include glucose, lipids, renal markers,
      liver-associated measurements, electrolytes, and other biomarkers.
    

    
      Determine whether fasting or examination-session restrictions apply.
      Review specimen type and analytical platform.
      Identify component-specific subsample weights.
      Check method-comparison or calibration guidance.
    
  

  
    Environmental exposure biomarkers

    
      Exposure components may measure metals, pesticides, volatile compounds,
      metabolites, or other environmental biomarkers.
    

    
      Review limits of detection and substitution rules.
      Identify dilution adjustments where relevant.
      Check batch, specimen, and storage considerations.
      Confirm the applicable laboratory subsample weight.
    
  

  
    Infectious disease testing

    
      Infectious disease components may include antibody, antigen,
      molecular, or other evidence of infection or immunity.
    

    
      Understand qualitative and quantitative result coding.
      Review confirmatory testing algorithms.
      Distinguish current infection, past exposure, and immunity.
      Check age and specimen-availability restrictions.
    
  

  
    Nutrition biomarkers

    
      Nutrition laboratory components may include vitamins, minerals,
      metabolites, and other indicators of nutritional status.
    

    
      Review fasting, supplement use, and collection timing.
      Check specimen stability and assay changes.
      Assess biomarker-specific reference considerations.
      Identify the appropriate survey weight and analytical sample.
    
  






Before using a laboratory variable


  
    Find the component
    Identify the correct file, cycle, and variable.
  

  
    Read the documentation
    Review units, method, eligibility, flags, and notes.
  

  
    Validate the data
    Inspect structure, keys, missingness, and value ranges.
  

  
    Define the analysis
    Select the population, weight, cycles, and interpretation.
  




Anatomy of a laboratory variable
A laboratory variable should be understood through more than its short name.

Variable identityMeasurement contextReported resultAnalytical population


Review:

variable name;
descriptive label;
source file;
survey cycle;
component;
specimen type.



Review:

analytical method;
instrument or platform;
calibration;
laboratory site;
specimen handling;
quality-control procedures.



Review:

unit;
valid range;
categorical coding;
result flags;
comment codes;
missing-value conventions.



Review:

age eligibility;
examination status;
fasting requirements;
subsample selection;
valid survey weight;
missing-result patterns.






Laboratory detection limits
Some laboratory components include values below a method’s detection limit.
The released data may provide:

a reported result variable;
a detection-limit indicator;
a lower detection limit;
an imputed or substituted result;
cycle-specific analytical guidance.







WarningDo not invent a universal substitution rule



Rules such as:
LOD / √2
or:
LOD / 2
may be appropriate in some contexts but should not be applied automatically.
Use the component documentation, analytical objective, distribution, and sensitivity analysis to justify the treatment of values below detection.




Missing laboratory values
A missing result may indicate:

the participant was not eligible;
the participant did not attend the MEC examination;
the specimen was not collected;
specimen volume was insufficient;
the assay failed;
the result was excluded during quality review;
the analyte was not measured in that cycle;
the participant was not selected for the subsample.

The meaning of missingness should be investigated before excluding records.


Case study: CBC and Demographic data


  From separate source files to an analysis-ready CBC dataset

  
    The CBC and Demographic pipeline demonstrates how laboratory science,
    data engineering, and survey methodology work together.
  

  

    
      Source decision
      
        Identify the primary CBC source for every survey cycle.
      
    

    
      Repeat examination
      
        Preserve the 2001–2002 second CBC examination separately.
      
    

    
      Participant key
      
        Merge CBC and Demographic records using survey cycle plus SEQN.
      
    

    
      Scientific output
      
        Produce validated datasets, summaries, figures, and provenance records.
      
    

  




Laboratory quality and analytical quality
Laboratory quality assurance and data-analysis quality are related but distinct.

Laboratory quality assuranceData-analysis quality assuranceShared objective


May include:

calibration;
control materials;
proficiency testing;
instrument maintenance;
reagent review;
specimen acceptance;
corrective action;
analytical performance monitoring.



May include:

source validation;
cycle tracking;
variable harmonization;
duplicate investigation;
merge validation;
missingness review;
weight selection;
reproducibility records.



Both systems aim to ensure that:
the reported result is accurate,
traceable,
interpretable,
and fit for its intended use





Common laboratory-data mistakes






WarningMistake 1: Selecting a variable by name alone



The variable’s method, unit, eligibility, and cycle documentation must also be reviewed.








WarningMistake 2: Assuming every participant has every laboratory result



Laboratory eligibility, examination completion, specimen availability, and subsampling affect record availability.








WarningMistake 3: Combining cycles without reviewing method changes



A consistent variable name does not prove analytical comparability.








WarningMistake 4: Ignoring detection-limit variables



Reported values near or below detection may require specific analytical treatment.








WarningMistake 5: Using the wrong survey weight



The weight must represent the smallest eligible sample associated with the laboratory variables used.




Laboratory-data knowledge check






NoteIs a laboratory variable name sufficient to establish comparability across cycles?





No. Review the method, units, eligibility, instrument, documentation, and cycle-specific analytical guidance.









NoteWhy might a participant have no laboratory result?





They may have been ineligible, absent from the examination, missing a specimen, excluded during quality review, or outside the selected subsample.









NoteShould repeat examinations be appended automatically to the primary laboratory file?





No. Their analytical role and eligibility must be investigated first.









NoteWhat information should remain attached to an imported laboratory record?





At minimum, retain the survey cycle, source file, component, participant identifier, and file role.









NoteDoes a correct assay result automatically produce a valid population estimate?





No. Population inference also requires correct eligibility, data integration, survey weighting, and design-based analysis.





Laboratory-data checklist
Before analyzing an NHANES laboratory component, confirm:

The correct component and source file are identified.
The survey cycle is retained.
The participant identifier is present.
The meaning of one row is understood.
Primary and supplementary records are distinguished.
Variable labels and units are verified.
Laboratory methods have been reviewed.
Instrument or platform changes have been considered.
Detection-limit variables have been identified.
Missing-value meaning has been investigated.
Eligibility criteria are documented.
The correct survey weight is identified.
Strata and PSU variables are available.
Cross-cycle comparability has been assessed.
Analytical limitations are documented.
Provenance is preserved.

Participants are concentrated within a small number of geographic clusters.
Even though both samples contain 1,000 records, Sample B may contain less independent information.

ImportantSample size alone does not determine precision



A complex survey may have the same number of observations as a simple random sample but a different variance because of clustering, stratification, unequal selection probabilities, and weighting.

Component onboarding pathway
Every new component should pass through four broad stages.


  
    1
    Scope
    
      Define the component, cycles, research purpose, and analytical population.
    
  

  
    2
    Scientific review
    
      Assess eligibility, methods, units, record structure, and weights.
    
  

  
    3
    Implementation
    
      Build manifests, crosswalks, scripts, validation rules, and outputs.
    
  

  
    4
    Release
    
      Test, document, review, publish, and assign validated status.
    
  




Component onboarding requirements


  
    1. Source manifest
    Minimum fields:
    
      component
      survey_cycle
      file_name
      source_url
      record_level
      expected_key
      analytic_role
    
  

  
    2. Variable crosswalk
    Minimum fields:
    
      survey_cycle
      source_variable
      harmonized_variable
      label
      unit
      method
      decision
      notes

      eligible ages;
      sex restrictions;
      pregnancy restrictions;
      examination requirements;
      fasting requirements;
      subsample selection;
      collection-session restrictions.
    
  

  
    4. Laboratory-method review
    
      specimen type;
      instrument;
      method;
      laboratory;
      detection limits;
      quality-control notes;
      corrections;
      comparability decisions.
    
  

  
    5. Weight guidance
    
      candidate interview or MEC weight;
      specialized subsample weight;
      multi-cycle construction;
      exclusions;
      limitations.
    
  

  
    6. Record-level contract
    
      one record per participant;
      multiple records per participant;
      repeat examinations;
      replicate measurements;
      specimen-level records.
    
  

  
    7. Validation rules
    
      source-file existence;
      HTTP success;
      expected variables;
      expected key;
      key uniqueness where required;
      cycle consistency;
      row-count review;
      missingness review;
      join-contract testing.
    
  

  
    8. Required outputs

      optional CSV;
      provenance manifest;
      validation summary;
      duplicate report;
      unresolved-conflict report;
      package-version record;
      session information.

How development priorities are selected


  
    Public-health relevance
    
      Does the component support important clinical, epidemiological, or policy questions?
    
  

  
    Cycle availability
    
      Is the component available across enough cycles to support useful analysis?
    
  

  
    Methodological complexity
    
      Are methods, eligibility, weights, and harmonization manageable?
    
  

  
    Learner demand
    
      Is there clear educational or analytical interest in the component?
    
  

  
    Architectural fit
    
      Can the component use or extend the current pipeline structure?
    
  

  
    Documentation quality
    
      Are official files, methods, eligibility notes, and weight guidance available?
    
  

  
    Scientific collaboration
    
      Is suitable subject-matter expertise available for review?
    
  




Requesting a component
Before proposing a new laboratory pipeline, identify:

the desired laboratory component;
the survey cycles;
the primary research question;
required supporting variables;
the intended population;
whether weighted national inference is required.

Requests may be submitted through the project’s GitHub issue tracker.

WarningThis catalog is a roadmap, not an analytical authorization



It does not replace:

Protected merge
Conceptual merge:
cbc_demo_merged <- cbc_primary |>
  dplyr::inner_join(
    demo_data,
    by = c(

title: NHANES CBC and Demographic Data Pipeline in R
text:
Pre-merge anti-joins
CBC records without Demographics:
cbc_without_demo <- cbc_primary |>
  dplyr::anti_join(
    demo_data,
    by = c(
      "survey_cycle",
      "SEQN"
    )
  )
Demographic records without CBC:
demo_without_cbc <- demo_data |>
  dplyr::anti_join(
    cbc_primary,
    by = c(
      "survey_cycle",
      "SEQN"
    )
  )
The second anti-join is expected to contain many records because not every Demographic participant necessarily has a valid CBC record.
The first anti-join requires careful review because each CBC record should ordinarily link to its participant’s Demographic record.

Important duplicate-handling principle
The 2001–2002 release includes:

L25_B, the primary CBC examination;
L25_2_B, a second CBC examination.

The same participant can appear in both files.
Appending the two files by rows can therefore create duplicate participant keys.






WarningDo not use this as a shortcut



dplyr::distinct(
  SEQN,
  .keep_all = TRUE
)
This code keeps one arbitrary participant row and discards the others.
It does not determine whether the other records are:

exact duplicates;
repeat measurements;
complementary records;
conflicting records.

The tutorial investigates the scientific meaning before deciding what to retain in the primary analytical dataset.

title: Lesson 8: Download All Required NHANES Files
text:
Create a safe wrapper
The download_nhanes_file() function stops when one file fails.
For a bulk process, we want to:

record the failure;
continue to the next file;
review all results afterward.

Create a safe wrapper:
download_catalog_row <- function(
    dataset_id,
    cycle,
    component,
    file_id,
    analysis_role,
    url,
    local_destination,
    overwrite = FALSE) {

  started_at <- Sys.time()

  result <- tryCatch(
    {
      local_file <- download_nhanes_file(
        url = url,
        destination = local_destination,
        overwrite = overwrite
      )

      file_information <- file.info(
        local_file
      )

      file_hash <- digest::digest(
        local_file,
        algorithm = "sha256",
        file = TRUE
      )

      tibble::tibble(
        dataset_id = dataset_id,
        cycle = cycle,
        component = component,
        file_id = file_id,
        analysis_role = analysis_role,
        source_url = url,
        local_file = local_file,
        status = "success",
        file_size_bytes = unname(
          file_information$size
        ),
        sha256 = file_hash,
        error_message = NA_character_,
        started_at_utc = format(
          started_at,
          tz = "UTC",
          usetz = TRUE
        ),
        completed_at_utc = format(
          Sys.time(),
          tz = "UTC",
          usetz = TRUE
        )
      )
    },
    error = function(error_condition) {
      tibble::tibble(
        dataset_id = dataset_id,
        cycle = cycle,
        component = component,
        file_id = file_id,
        analysis_role = analysis_role,
        source_url = url,
        local_file = local_destination,
        status = "failed",
        file_size_bytes = NA_real_,
        sha256 = NA_character_,
        error_message = conditionMessage(
          error_condition
        ),
        started_at_utc = format(
          started_at,
          tz = "UTC",
          usetz = TRUE
        ),
        completed_at_utc = format(
          Sys.time(),
          tz = "UTC",
          usetz = TRUE
        )
      )
    }
  )

  result
}

Why compare only shared variables?

title: Lesson 10: Investigate and Handle Duplicate Records
text:
Build a value-comparison function
Create:
values_equal_with_missing <- function(
    first_value,
    second_value) {

  dplyr::case_when(
    is.na(first_value) &
      is.na(second_value) ~ TRUE,

    is.na(first_value) |
      is.na(second_value) ~ FALSE,

    TRUE ~ first_value ==
      second_value
  )
}

text:
Compare each shared participant across common variables
Create a long comparison table:
shared_measurement_comparison <-
  purrr::map_dfr(
    measurement_variables,
    function(variable_name) {

      primary_column <- paste0(
        variable_name,
        "_primary"
      )

      second_column <- paste0(
        variable_name,
        "_second"
      )

      tibble::tibble(
        SEQN =
          shared_second_exam_comparison$SEQN,
        variable =
          variable_name,
        primary_value =
          shared_second_exam_comparison[[
            primary_column
          ]],
        second_exam_value =
          shared_second_exam_comparison[[
            second_column
          ]],
        values_match =
          values_equal_with_missing(
            shared_second_exam_comparison[[
              primary_column
            ]],
            shared_second_exam_comparison[[
              second_column
            ]]
          )
      )
    }
  )
Inspect:

  n = 50
)

  shared_measurement_comparison |>
  dplyr::group_by(
    variable
  ) |>
  dplyr::summarise(
    compared_participants =
      dplyr::n(),
    matching_values =
      sum(
        values_match,
        na.rm = TRUE
      ),
    different_values =
      sum(
        !values_match,
        na.rm = TRUE
      ),
    percent_different =
      100 *
      different_values /
      compared_participants,
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  dplyr::arrange(
    dplyr::desc(
      different_values
    ),
    variable
  )

title: Lesson 10: Investigate and Handle Duplicate Records

Create a participant-level summary:
second_exam_participant_comparison <-
  shared_measurement_comparison |>
  dplyr::group_by(
    SEQN
  ) |>
  dplyr::summarise(
    compared_variables =
      dplyr::n(),
    matching_variables =
      sum(
        values_match,
        na.rm = TRUE
      ),
    different_variables =
      sum(
        !values_match,
        na.rm = TRUE
      ),
    all_common_values_match =
      all(
        values_match
      ),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    comparison_class =
      dplyr::case_when(
        all_common_values_match ~
          "all_common_values_match",

        different_variables > 0 ~
          "different_measurements",

        TRUE ~
          "unresolved"
      )
  )
Inspect:

  n = Inf
)

title: Lesson 10: Investigate and Handle Duplicate Records

all_common_values_match
All compared common values are identical.
This is evidence of a value-level match across the shared variables.
It does not justify deleting the supplementary source because:

source roles differ;
source provenance differs;
nonshared variables may differ;
the records belong to separate examination contexts.



different_measurements
At least one common variable differs between the primary and second examinations.
This indicates that the second record contains distinct measurements.


unresolved
The comparison could not be classified completely.
This category should be preserved and investigated.

Deleting the second examination

Using distinct(SEQN, .keep_all = TRUE)
This keeps an arbitrary record without scientific justification.


Comparing every column directly
Pipeline metadata and source-specific variables may differ even when scientific measurements match.


Calling all shared participants exact duplicates
The same participant appearing in both files does not mean the measurement values are identical.

Identical values across shared variables do not erase differences in source role, examination context, or nonshared variables.

section: Variable names, labels, and factor levels
text:
Variable names, labels, and factor levels
These three concepts are different.

Variable name
Used directly in R code:
RIAGENDR


Variable label
Describes the meaning of the variable:
Gender


Factor labels
Describe individual coded values:
1 = Male
2 = Female
A well-documented analytical dataset can preserve all three.

title: Lesson 14: Create Readable Variable Labels
Lesson 14: Create Readable Variable Labels
text:
Common mistakes

Renaming all NHANES variables immediately
This makes it harder to compare the data with official documentation and published code.


Replacing coded variables with factors
Keep the original source variable and create a derived readable version.


Writing labels from memory
Use the imported label or official documentation.


Assuming every unlabelled variable is wrong
Pipeline-created variables may simply require locally defined labels.


Treating labels as harmonization evidence
A common label does not prove that units, methods, or eligibility are consistent across cycles.


Losing labels during export
CSV files do not preserve R variable-label attributes.
Save an RDS dataset and a separate variable dictionary.

Knowledge check






NoteWhy should original NHANES variable names be preserved?





They correspond to official documentation, support reproducibility, and make it easier to compare the pipeline with other NHANES code and publications.









NoteWhy create sex instead of replacing RIAGENDR?





RIAGENDR preserves the original coded source variable, while sex provides a readable factor for analysis and presentation.









NoteDoes assigning the same label across cycles prove that a variable is harmonized?





No. Harmonization also requires review of units, methods, eligibility, coding, specimen type, and documentation.

What this lesson prepares
Lesson 17 will use the outputs from this lesson to create four figures:

Mean hemoglobin trend by survey cycle and sex
Hemoglobin distribution by survey cycle and sex
Analytical record counts by survey cycle and sex
Hemoglobin missingness by survey cycle and sex

The first figure will be the principal result.

Important statistical scope
All summaries in this lesson are:
unweighted descriptive summaries
They describe the analytical records in the dataset.
They are not automatically nationally representative.
Formal NHANES population estimates require:

the appropriate examination or subsample weight;
SDMVSTRA;
SDMVPSU;
correct multi-cycle weight construction;
complex-survey variance estimation.







WarningDo not describe these results as national estimates



The analyses in this lesson are designed to demonstrate the completed data pipeline and prepare professional exploratory figures.
They should be described as:
unweighted descriptive summaries of the analytical records
They should not be described as:
nationally representative hemoglobin estimates

The calculation:
mean ± 1.96 × standard error
treats the records as though they came from a simple random sample.
NHANES uses a complex, multistage survey design.
The variables in this lesson are therefore named:
lower_descriptive_95
upper_descriptive_95
rather than simply:
lower_95
upper_95
This reduces the risk that learners will mistake them for survey-adjusted confidence intervals.

section: Prepare scale recommendations for the principal figure
text:
Prepare scale recommendations for the principal figure
The principal graph should use a scale based on the observed descriptive intervals rather than an arbitrary range.
Calculate the displayed minimum and maximum:
trend_interval_minimum <- min(
  hemoglobin_trend_figure_data$lower_descriptive_95,
  na.rm = TRUE
)
trend_interval_maximum <- max(
  hemoglobin_trend_figure_data$upper_descriptive_95,
  na.rm = TRUE
)
Add a small amount of visual space:
trend_axis_padding <- max(
  0.5,
  0.10 *
    (
      trend_interval_maximum -
        trend_interval_minimum
    )
)
Create recommended limits:
trend_y_axis_lower <- floor(
  (
    trend_interval_minimum -
      trend_axis_padding
  ) *
    2
) /
  2
trend_y_axis_upper <- ceiling(
  (
    trend_interval_maximum +
      trend_axis_padding
  ) *
    2
) /
  2
Choose an appropriate break interval:
trend_y_axis_range <-
  trend_y_axis_upper -
    trend_y_axis_lower
trend_y_axis_break <- dplyr::case_when(
  trend_y_axis_range <= 3 ~
    0.5,

  trend_y_axis_range <= 8 ~
    1,

  trend_y_axis_range <= 15 ~
    2,

  TRUE ~
    5
)
Create a scale summary:
hemoglobin_trend_scale_recommendation <-
  tibble::tibble(
    observed_interval_minimum =
      trend_interval_minimum,
    observed_interval_maximum =
      trend_interval_maximum,
    recommended_axis_lower =
      trend_y_axis_lower,
    recommended_axis_upper =
      trend_y_axis_upper,
    recommended_break_interval =
      trend_y_axis_break,
    recommendation =
      paste(
        "Use the data-informed range for readability,",
        "state the unweighted scope clearly,",
        "and avoid interpreting visual differences as national estimates."
      )
  )
Inspect:
print(
  hemoglobin_trend_scale_recommendation
)






ImportantA focused y-axis must be transparent



The principal trend graph may use a focused range because it is intended to show relatively small differences in mean hemoglobin.
To avoid misleading readers:

the axis must be clearly numbered;
the scale must be based on the observed data;
the caption must identify the descriptive scope;
the figure must not imply that zero is the meaningful reference point;
the selected limits must not hide any mean or interval.

text:
How to describe the results
Appropriate language:
Hemoglobin was summarized descriptively among complete analytical records
by two-year NHANES survey cycle and sex. All results are unweighted.
Avoid:
National hemoglobin levels increased or decreased over time.
That statement would require correctly weighted complex-survey analysis.

title: Lesson 16: Analyze and Prepare Hemoglobin Data for Visualization
Lesson 16: Analyze and Prepare Hemoglobin Data for Visualization
text:
Common mistakes

Preparing only a mean table
A mean does not reveal the full distribution, record count, or missingness pattern.


Reporting descriptive intervals as survey confidence intervals
The intervals in this lesson do not incorporate the NHANES complex sampling design.


Removing extreme values automatically
Flag and investigate unusual values before exclusion.


Ignoring changes in analytical record count
A group mean based on fewer records may be less stable.


Ignoring missingness
Changes in missingness can affect comparisons across cycles.


Using an arbitrary graph scale
The principal figure will use a scale derived from the displayed means and intervals.


Interpreting sex differences causally
The summaries are unadjusted and descriptive.


Describing unweighted records as the U.S. population
National inference requires survey weights and design variables.

Knowledge check






NoteWhy prepare more than one figure?





The mean trend shows the central pattern, but the distribution, record-count, and missingness figures reveal information that a mean-only graph can hide.









NoteWhy are the interval variables named lower_descriptive_95 and upper_descriptive_95?





The names make clear that the intervals are conventional unweighted descriptive intervals rather than NHANES survey-adjusted confidence intervals.









NoteWhy calculate the principal figure scale from the observed data?





A data-informed scale includes all displayed means and intervals, avoids arbitrary choices, and supports a readable figure without hiding observations.









NoteCan a visually polished figure be considered a nationally representative result?





No. Visual quality does not replace appropriate survey weighting, design specification, and complex-survey variance estimation.

Why use a clean session?
A script can appear to work because objects from previous interactive work remain in memory.

Using Rscript starts a separate R process and reduces dependence on the current VS Code session.
